sink: child_process.exec(wgetCommand) -- runs the whole string through /bin/sh -c
why: wgetCommand is built by string-concatenating caller-controlled url and outputPath (isValidDownloadArgs only checks typeof, no content validation) into a single command line and passed to exec(), which spawns a shell. outputPath has zero escaping: '--directory-prefix=' + outputPath, so outputPath='; touch /tmp/pwned #' injects an arbitrary second shell command. url is passed through `new URL(url)` first, but that only validates it parses as a URL -- characters like `$`, `(`, `)`, `;`, `&`, backtick are all legal, unencoded URI characters, so url="http://a.com/$(touch /tmp/pwned)" also achieves the same injection through the trailing bare `url` argument in the command array.
contract: Download an entire website using wget

sink: subprocess.run(["osascript", "-e", applescript]) where applescript embeds script inside a double-quoted `do javascript "..."` AppleScript string
guard: bypassable: a literal backslash immediately followed by a double-quote in `code` survives as `\\"` in the output, which AppleScript parses as an escaped-backslash followed by an UNESCAPED closing quote
why: Running caller-supplied ExtendScript inside Illustrator is this tool's stated purpose, so that alone is not the finding. The finding is that the quote-escaping meant to keep `code` confined inside the `do javascript "..."` string literal is bypassable: str.replace('"','\\"') blindly replaces every raw `"` with `\\"` regardless of what precedes it, so if `code` already contains a literal backslash immediately before a `"`, that pair becomes `\\\\"` -- wait, concretely: input characters backslash+quote (2 chars) become backslash+backslash+quote (3 chars) after the replace, i.e. `\\\"`. AppleScript reads the first two backslashes as one escaped literal backslash, leaving the following quote unescaped, which closes the string early. Everything in `code` after that point is then parsed as literal AppleScript source, not as the JS payload string -- letting a caller inject arbitrary additional AppleScript, e.g. `tell application \"Terminal\" to do script \"<any shell command>\"`, which is full OS command execution outside Illustrator's own JS sandbox.
Zero-argument tool; only runs a fixed AppleScript activation script and a fixed screencapture command with no caller input.

sink: eval()/exec() of caller-supplied code with self.locals containing the real __builtins__ (no restriction), i.e. the full Python standard library and OS access
why: This tool's declared purpose is an interactive Python REPL, so running caller-given code is expected -- but unlike githejie/mcp-server-calculator's AST-whitelist evaluator elsewhere in this corpus, this REPL is completely unsandboxed: `self.locals = {"__builtins__": builtins}` grants the full builtins (open, __import__, os via import, subprocess via import, etc.), so any caller (including a prompt-injected agent that only meant to compute something) gets unrestricted file read/write, network access, subprocess execution, and can read this MCP server process's own environment variables. Filed Tier B rather than A because 'run my code' is the stated contract, but the complete absence of any sandbox exceeds what a reasonable caller of a scripting tool would expect and matches the rubric's carve-out for that case.
contract: Interactive Python REPL that maintains session state.
